short: The late empire, rebuilt as an openly autocratic state — and, in the west, the last two centuries of it.
full:
Diocletian stopped pretending. Where the princeps had been first citizen, the late emperor was dominus, lord, approached through ceremony that put a distance between him and everyone else. The provinces were cut into smaller pieces and grouped into dioceses, the army was reorganised into frontier troops and a mobile field force, and taxation was rebuilt to pay for both.

The other change was Christianity. Diocletian persecuted the church harder than any emperor before him; within a decade of his abdication Constantine had legalised it, and by the end of the century it was the religion of the state. Constantine also founded a second capital at Byzantium, which mattered more than anyone could have known at the time.

The halves drifted apart. After 395 they were never again ruled by one man. The east kept its revenues, its walls and its bureaucracy; the west spent the fifth century paying for armies it could not afford, ceding provinces to federate kings, and watching real power pass to its own generals. In 476 the last western emperor was deposed and no replacement was appointed. The east carried on for another thousand years.
